transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

Um, I guess... I guess they brought me in because of what has been happening down at work. I work at this big freight warehouse, you know, moving materials and stocking pallets. I was taking some college classes a while back, but now I am just doing the warehouse thing, and it gets really, really loud in there with all the machinery. But lately, well, my supervisor got really upset because I keep doing things out on the floor. 

Like, I will be right by the forklift, and I just... I have to stop. I freeze. My arms go all the way up in the air, and I just stand there completely frozen with my arms pointing up by the machine. And the forklift, when it backs up, it makes this loud warning noise, so I started copying the beeping sounds. I make the sounds right back at it, exactly the same pitch, and I copy the hand signals the floor spotters use, just doing them over and over while I am frozen there. 

And then with the freight itself, the boxes, I can not just stack them normally anymore. I have been moving the boxes in these strange little patterns on the floor. It is very specific, the way they have to go, these tiny little geometric patterns instead of just loading them up. And the whole time I am doing this, making the sounds and moving the boxes in my patterns, all the other guys and the floor manager are just yelling at me. They are yelling for me to stop, telling me to get back to work and put my hands down, just screaming over the noise of the warehouse, but I do not stop. I just keep doing the patterns and the beeping anyway even when everyone is yelling. So they did not like that at all. I guess that is why they made me come see you today.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people don't seem to hear or see?

No... no, I don't think so. I mean, the warehouse is so loud, right? There's the forklifts, and the conveyor belts, and the big metal doors rolling up and down on their tracks. It's just a constant roar of noise, like this heavy, grinding sound that gets inside your head. But the sounds I hear, like the beeping of the forklift backing up, everyone hears that. That's why I copy it, because it's right there, echoing off the high ceilings. 

And the boxes, they're just normal boxes. Brown cardboard, mostly. Sometimes they have those heavy-duty staples in the sides or thick plastic strapping around them. I see the same boxes everyone else sees. I just... I see how they need to be arranged on the floor, you know? Like, the angles and the spaces between them. But I'm not seeing ghosts or hearing voices whispering to me from the rafters or anything like that. Just the regular warehouse stuff, the same stuff the floor manager is looking at when he's yelling at me. It's just that I interact with it differently now. So, no, I'm not seeing or hearing anything that isn't actually there in the building with us. It's all real. It's all just the freight and the machinery.
How has your mood been feeling lately?

My mood? Um, I don't know, I guess... I guess it's just been normal? I mean, what is normal anyway, right? But I haven't really been feeling sad or crying or anything like that. I don't wake up feeling down in the dumps. I just wake up, and I get ready for work, and I go to the warehouse. I put on my steel-toed boots, the brown ones with the scuff marks on the toes from where I accidentally kicked a pallet jack last month, and I pack my lunch—usually just a turkey sandwich with mustard, no mayo because mayo goes bad if it sits in the breakroom fridge too long and the fridge has this weird hum to it anyway—and I just go. 

I don't feel angry, either, not really. Even when the floor manager is yelling at me, his face getting all red and the veins popping out on his neck, and all the other guys are staring... I don't feel mad at them. I don't feel happy, exactly, but I'm not depressed. I just feel like I'm there, doing what I have to do with the boxes and the patterns and the beeping. It's just... I'm just existing in the space, you know? Like I'm just part of the warehouse machinery, moving along with the conveyor belts and the rolling doors. So, yeah, my mood hasn't really been anything specific. It's just kind of flat, I guess, or just... just regular. I haven't really noticed feeling one way or another, just focused on the forklift sounds and getting the angles right on the cardboard.
Have you been diagnosed with any physical medical conditions or had any recent physical illnesses?

No, no, I haven't been sick. I mean, physically sick, like with a fever or a cough or anything like that. I haven't been to a regular doctor in... well, I don't even know how long. Maybe since I was doing those college classes and I had to get a physical for something, but that was a while ago before I started at the warehouse full time. 

I don't have asthma or diabetes or high blood pressure or any of those things people take pills for every morning. My body works fine. My arms work fine, obviously, since I can hold them up by the forklift like I do, just completely still for a really long time. You have to be in pretty good physical shape to hold your arms locked up in the air like that without dropping them, especially when the forklift is right there backing up and beeping. And my back is fine from lifting all those boxes, all the heavy cardboard ones with the strapping. 

Sometimes I get a little sore, you know, just in the shoulders right around the shoulder blades, from moving the boxes into the patterns on the floor, because you have to bend down at a very specific angle to get the geometry right, to make sure the corners line up perfectly on the concrete. The concrete is always so cold and dusty, and it has these little cracks running through it that you have to pay attention to when you're setting the boxes down. But that's just normal soreness, not a medical condition. I don't get headaches or stomachaches, even when I eat the turkey sandwiches every day. So, no, my body is totally fine. Nothing physically wrong with me at all, no illnesses or anything like that. Just the regular warehouse wear and tear on the boots, but not on me.
About how long ago did you first start experiencing this freezing, copying sounds, and arranging things in patterns?

Well... let me think about that. How long... I guess it's been about six months now? Yeah, six months. I know this because it was right around the time they started bringing in the winter freight, all those heavy boxes with the space heaters and the thermal gear that have the thicker plastic strapping on them. They always smell a little bit like ozone and dust. That was six months ago. 

That's when I first realized that the boxes couldn't just be stacked any old way, that they had to be arranged in those specific patterns on the cold concrete to match the cracks. If you don't line them up, the whole space feels wrong. And the freezing... that started then too, because when the forklift backs up—the big yellow one, not the smaller electric ones they use over in aisle four, but the heavy-duty one—when that specific one backs up, the sound just demands that you stop and become part of the machinery. So I'd lock my arms up, just like the forks, and make the beeping sound so it echoes right. 

And it's been six months of doing that. The floor manager, he's been getting so angry for six months, telling me my behavior is strange and that my talking is confusing. He says he doesn't understand what I'm saying when I try to explain the geometry of the cardboard to him, or why the pitch of the beep means I have to hold my arms perfectly still. He just crosses his arms and his neck gets all red, and he tells the other guys I'm talking nonsense. So, yeah, it's been about six months of the strange behavior and the confusing talking, at least that's what they call it at the warehouse. To me, it's just what I've been doing for the last six months to make sure everything fits together the way it's supposed to.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with prominent catatonic psychomotor disturbances that have persisted for approximately 6 months, leading to marked workplace dysfunction. Symptoms include catatonic stupor/posturing (freezing in place with arms raised), echolalia (vocal imitation of forklift beeping), echopraxia (repetitive imitation of hand signals), bizarre stereotypies/mannerisms (arranging boxes into rigid geometric patterns), and negativism (unresponsiveness to demands to stop), meeting the ICD-10 criteria for catatonic schizophrenia (F20.2).
